Chungking
Now. 5, 1938
Personal and Confidential
Mr. H. M. Bixby
Pan American Airways
New York, No Y.
Dear Bix:
Your long personal letter of Oct. 17th was received yesterday, coming up
on the plane from Hong Kong that morning• I am enclosing in this envelope another
personal letter which I had written to you two days ago but am writing this now
to reply to some specific questions raised in your letter and also because I was
glad to get your letter and I feel inspired to answer it•
With the experience I have had in the New York office and with what you
mentioned I can easily imagine the general situation just now although no doubt I
do not do the subject full justice. I have my troubles but I will keep them and
you can have yours•
In a letter to Mr. Morgan written last night and going forward by this
mail I outlined our present general situation particularly with respect to getting
into Hanoi, a point mentioned in your letter. I will only add that we are fully
alive to the inherent risks connected with flying into Hongkong under the present
conditions and we are doing and have been doing all possible to complete the
necessary arrangements to fly into Hanoi. I have personally discussed the matter
with DR. Kung, I.V. Soong and the Minister of Communications. I started on Aug. 24th
the day Woods was shot down and have been following it up closely. It would take the
weoght of several years off of me to get into Hanoi just now. I think we will but
I do not know when.
Referring to your comments on CNAC being behind schedule in payments I
am glad to say that thas condition has greatly improved since you wrote your letter.
We have collected for the two cyclone engines, the DCIwo center section, have
completed the payments on the Commodores and have added about US$LO,000.00
to
CNAC's fixed deposit making a total deposit of approximately US$20.000.00. This
however I am afraid is about as far as I can go, except of course, getting the money
for spare parts orders when they arrive in Hongkong•
Regarding tka credits through
the American Export & Import Bank it would of course be very helpful but it seems
to me the detail for such an arrangement would be tremendous and there is really no
telling what obstacles the Ministry would put in the way. They certainly would want
a percent for permitting the credit.
I know of a foreign group who had the reputation
and the capital who approached the Ministry of Communications recently with an offer
to put twenty new three ton truck into service out of Kunming, freight there is
piling up terribly, if the Ministry would give them free rights during the war.
The
Minister demanded twenty percent of the gross revenúe as a tax for the Ministry and
stuck to it and the deal fell through. You would think that as great as their need for
transportation is now
a responsible trucking company would be offered a subsidy.
Also I do not think the situation out here is such that any one could offer credit to

we have been for the past year. It is not much of a system but at least we know
we have to depend on our own efforts and we act accordingly. I do not put much
trust in anything else just now.
Regarding your suggestion that it might be possible to carry silk from
Chungking
into Hongkong and make enough off of the exchange to profit by it, we
considered several such schemes but they are not practicable. Our planes
have to pass a very rigid Customs inspection now both at Chungking going and coming
and also in Hongkong by Chinese Inspectors. Also the Chinese Government has taken
over all import and export business and you must have a permit for each shipment•
We would have to have a permit for each shipment, giving all details and the price
must be in foreign currency. Collections must be paid, in foreign currency to the
Ministry of Finance, or Central Trust, who will remit to the shipper or vendor in
National Currency at the official rate. The profit on the exchenge goes to the
Ministry of Finance.
Regarding the Clipper continuing to fly into Hongkong I agree with you
fully that the situation has not been changed by the occupation of South China and
no change in policy is called for. In fact as you say as the Japanese move inland
into South China there will be less flying around over the ocean by Japanese planes.
and the Clipper will come in behind the flying.
However this is only a principle and
does not cover all the details. The Japanese navgy no doubt will continue to have
a carrier outside and will fly planes from it.
That is certain but at least the
situation is no worse. However since you asked me I would like to offef one
suggestion.
I understand PAA does not advise
the Japanese in anyway regarding their
schedules and flights. I may be misinformed but anyway I think they should. I do
not think any sovereign right is involved nor would I be too much of a stickler
if it was.
I am in complete disagreement with those who maintain that since no
war has been these declared there is no war and the
Japanese exxx cannot do certain
things which they might have the right to do if war had been declared.
entirely by what I have seen I am convinced there is a war and the theorist can say
what they choose• Also the war is absolutely vital to the Japanese and they are
taking it very seriously• Also in spite of many cases of individual, and collective,
as the Germans or the English did before we got into the world war, and probably mor
than the French and English did after we got into it. However that
is not important.
If PAA regularly advises the Japanese of their schedules and flights in my opinion
it will be a very decided added safety factor and that is of the utmost importance.
Regarding Allison I can easily understand how difficult it is for PAA to
place kim a man of his position on short notice.
I think
Allison appreciates
that but the offer which PAA did make him immediately after the war was made at a
time when his wife was having a baby and everything was in confusion and it not
register very clearly with him at that time and unfortunately it never has properly
registered.
Allie has a rather single track mind as you know. An admirable taait
in some respects but rather difficult at times in others. i have told him that
if and when he gets back to the States he goes to see PAA he will be surprised
at the cordial welcome he will get and pleased with the efforts that will be made
in his behalf.
